questions.question: A green-threads library multiplexes 50 user threads over a single kernel thread; the moment one thread issues a blocking read, all 50 stall together. Which threading model is this?
questions.explanation: With many user threads on one kernel thread, the kernel sees a single schedulable entity, so one blocking syscall freezes the whole bundle — the classic many-to-one weakness.

questions.question: On a modern Linux or Windows box, every user thread maps to its own kernel thread, so one thread's blocking syscall leaves its siblings running — at the price of a kernel object per thread. Which model is this?
questions.explanation: One-to-one threading gives each user thread a kernel thread, providing true concurrency and independent blocking, but making each thread cost kernel resources.

questions.question: A language runtime multiplexes 200 user threads over a pool of 8 kernel threads: a blocking call stalls only a few, yet the pool still runs in parallel across cores. Which threading model is this?
questions.explanation: The many-to-many model multiplexes M user threads onto N kernel threads (M > N), combining user-level flexibility with kernel-level parallelism and graceful blocking.

questions.question: A shell forks a child: parent and child initially share all 100 memory pages read-only, and the kernel copies a page only when either side writes it. The child writes 12 pages before exec. How many of the 100 pages are still shared by both processes afterward?
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write shares pages until a write faults, and only written pages are copied. The child wrote 12, so those were duplicated and 100 - 12 = 88 pages remain shared.

questions.question: A minimal shell needs a child that will immediately exec(); it uses a fork variant that borrows the parent's address space outright and suspends the parent until the child execs or exits. Which call is it?
questions.explanation: vfork() skips copying entirely because the child is expected to exec at once; the parent sleeps until exec or exit so the child can't corrupt its address space.

questions.question: glibc's pthread_create must produce an execution context that shares its creator's address space, file-descriptor table, and signal handlers. Which Linux syscall, guided by its sharing flags, performs this?
questions.explanation: clone() takes CLONE_VM, CLONE_FILES, CLONE_SIGHAND and related flags controlling exactly what parent and child share — the machinery under Linux threads.

questions.question: The scheduler has picked task T to run, but the register save, stack switch, and jump into T's context are done by a different component. Which component finishes the context switch?
questions.explanation: The dispatcher executes the mechanics: saving state, switching stacks, restoring the new context, and jumping to user mode — after the scheduler decides who runs.

questions.question: Threads A and B corrupt a shared counter whenever their update loops interleave; the fix is to ensure the counter-updating code never runs in both at once. What is each such code region called?
questions.explanation: A critical section is the code touching shared state; mutual exclusion guarantees only one thread executes it at a time, eliminating the interleavings that corrupt the counter.

questions.question: Two threads in one process context-switch; the outgoing thread's registers, stack pointer, and program counter must be parked somewhere per-thread. In which kernel structure are they saved?
questions.explanation: Each thread owns a TCB holding its register image, stack pointer, PC, and scheduling info; switching threads means saving one TCB and loading another's.

questions.question: A single-threaded game loop drives 1,000 entity routines; each routine suspends itself with yield and resumes exactly where it left off, cooperating without any preemption. What are these constructs?
questions.explanation: Coroutines are cooperative execution contexts that suspend and resume at explicit yield points — many can live in one thread with no scheduler or locking needed between them.

questions.question: Inside the Linux kernel, one large C structure per process holds the state word, mm pointer, open-file table, and scheduling fields, all reachable from a global task list. Name that structure.
questions.explanation: task_struct is Linux's process descriptor: every process and thread has one, containing everything the kernel needs to schedule, signal, and manage the task.

questions.question: A daemon's children keep ending as zombies until it reaps them. Which signal does the kernel deliver to the daemon each time a child terminates, prompting it to call wait()?
questions.explanation: SIGCHLD tells a parent that a child changed state or exited; the handler typically loops on waitpid() to collect exit statuses and clear the zombies.

questions.question: If a program executes fork() three times in a row, how many total processes exist?
questions.explanation: Each fork() doubles the process count, so three calls give 2^3 = 8 processes. Every new child continues executing after the fork.

questions.question: A server process exits while three children are still running, and elsewhere a zombie lingers because its own parent died first. Which PID-1 process adopts the orphans and reaps the zombie?
questions.explanation: Orphans are reparented to PID 1 — init, or systemd/subreapers on modern Linux — which periodically calls wait() so no zombie accumulates under a dead parent.

questions.question: A host hits its per-user process limit; a program calls fork(), no child is created, and the call reports failure through errno. What return value signals the failure?
questions.explanation: fork() returns -1 on failure (e.g., EAGAIN for resource limits) with no child created; success returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent.

questions.question: A program executes the expression fork() && fork() || fork(). How many processes, including the original, exist afterward?
questions.explanation: Short-circuit evaluation leaves one process finishing via the parent path and four via the child paths, totaling 5.

questions.question: A program calls fork() once; only the child (where fork returns 0) then calls fork() once more. How many processes exist in total?
questions.explanation: The first fork creates parent plus child; the second fork, executed only by the child, adds one grandchild: 3 total.

questions.question: A process writes to a pipe whose read end has been closed in every process. What does the kernel deliver to the writer?
questions.explanation: Writing to a pipe with no readers raises SIGPIPE, which terminates the process by default; if caught, write() fails with EPIPE.

questions.question: A program prints its PID, then calls exec() to replace itself with a new binary. Inside the freshly loaded program, getpid() is called. What value does it return?
questions.explanation: exec() swaps the address space, code, and stack but keeps the same process — the PID, open descriptors, and parent are all preserved, so getpid() returns the original value.

questions.question: One thread of a multithreaded process calls exit(). What happens?
questions.explanation: exit() ends the whole process and all its threads; pthread_exit() terminates only the calling thread.
